title: Switching to Third-Line ART Regimens
tocPath: APPROACH TO PATIENTS WITH EMERGENCY CONDITIONS
Management of Adult and Adolescent Living with HIV with Antiretroviral Therapy

blocks.text: Before confirming virological failure of a second-line regimen, a Multidisciplinary Team (MDT) must convene to:
Rule out other causes of high viremia, including suboptimal adherence.
Plan for Enhanced Adherence Counseling (EAC) and provide necessary support to address adherence barriers.
If adherence barriers are fully resolved, viral re-suppression may occur, avoiding an unnecessary switch to a third-line regimen.

blocks.text: Requirements for Switching RoC to Third-Line ART
RoC must be failing second-line ART.
RoC must have completed EAC sessions and demonstrate good adherence.
There must be documented virological failure (VL ≥1,000 copies/ml) post-EAC.

IRIS is a phenomenon associated with the occurrence or worsening of opportunistic infections/malignancies which can occur early after initiation of ART or at later (several months) during ART. There is an increased risk for occurrence of IRIS in the following situations:

runs.text: occur early after initiation of ART or at later (several months) during ART. There is an increased risk for occurrence of IRIS in the following situations:

blocks.text: Patients with advanced HIV disease with CD4 cell count <50cells/mm3
Patients with undiagnosed and untreated opportunistic conditions
Patients who have been introduced on ART before or shortly after initiation of treatment of opportunistic infection/malignancy
In the advent of DTG use, there is increased likelihood for IRIS because of rapid HIV viral load suppression.
Note: Any OI, malignancy and autoimmune diseases may present as IRIS
The criteria for making a diagnosis of IRIS are delineated below
A typical presentation of “opportunistic infections or tumors” in patients responding to anti- retroviral therapy (ART) includes:
Localized disease e.g., lymph nodes, liver, spleen
Exaggerated inflammatory reaction e.g., severe fever, with exclusion of other causes of painful lesions
Atypical inflammatory response in affected tissues e.g., granulomas, suppuration, necrosis, perivascular lymphocytic inflammatory cell infiltrate

Progression of organ dysfunction or enlargement of pre-existing lesions after definite, clinical improvement with pathogen specific therapy prior to commencement of ART and exclusion of treatment toxicity and new diagnoses

Antiretroviral Therapy in Children and Adolescents Living with HIV
Maximally and durably suppress plasma HIV RNA (to <50 copies/ml)
Reduce HIV-associated morbidity and prolong the duration and quality of survival.

ART in children has been proven to increase survival and decrease HIV-related morbidity and mortality. Children should be started on ART as soon they are diagnosed including those who are presumably diagnosed.

Changing ART in Children Under 15 Years
Changing ART in Children is triggered by Drug Toxicity or Treatment failure
The principles for changing ARVs and the managing drug toxicity in children are like those applied to adults. Refer section

Virological treatment failure: Viral load is the most reliable method to detect early treatment failure. Virological treatment failure is recognized if the child is adherent to the current ART regimen, for 6months or more and has two consecutive viral load measurements of over 1000copies/ml at 3months apart.

Clinical Treatment Failure: Clinical conditions indicating that a change to second-line therapy is warranted include:
Poor growth (failure to gain weight, declining or stagnant weight) over a 6month period, after excluding other causes, such as TB, feeding problems and food/nutritional deficiency

blocks.text: Recurrent infections, such as oral candidiasis, persistent diarrhoea, recurrent severe bacterial pneumonia
Advancement from one clinical stage to another or new evidence of new WHO stage 3 or 4 disease
Short inter-current episodes of pneumonia, LRTI and gastroenteritis should not be regarded as clinical failure
Pulmonary or lymph node TB, which are clinical stage 3 conditions, are not indications of treatment failure, and thus may not require consideration of second-line therapy
